h1.u: 103 in view of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa

body.p: Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 43, 47, and 135-141 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Rylander, et al., U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2013/0338627 ("Rylander") in view of Szunerits, et al., "Sensing using Localised Surface Plasmon Resonance Sensors," Chem. Comm., 2012, 48, 8999-9010 ("Szunerits"), and further in view of Hosokawa, et al., Nanoparticle Technology Handbook, 2007, pg. 365. The Office Action alleges that Rylander generally teaches claim 1, except that Rylander does not teach at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member, wherein the at least one particle is positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to the end portion. The Office Action then alleges that such a particle is taught by Hosokawa.

It is submitted that the Patent Office has not acknowledged how or why one of ordinary skill in the art would have sought to have attached a particle to the device taught in Rylander such that the particle is positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to the end portion, as is recited in claim 1. While the Patent Office argues that "the concept of attaching nanoparticles to the end of optical fibers is not new," the Patent Office provides no evidentiary support for such a conclusion. Although the Patent Office points to Rylander, Rylander only describes a microneedle device, and does not teach or suggest that the microneedle device could have been modified by attaching nanoparticles to it-let alone attaching

the nanoparticles to it in such a way that the particles would have been positioned in an optically interrogatable position, as is explicitly claimed in claim 1. Indeed, for the reasons that follow, Rylander discourages and teaches away from attaching nanoparticles or anything else to the outside of the microneedles, let alone precisely positioned such that the nanoparticles would have been in optically interrogatable position with respect to the microneedle after the microneedles are forceably inserted through the skin.

Rylander is generally directed to a minimally invasive fiber optic microneedle device that physically penetrates tissue for light-based therapeutics (see, for example, paragraph [0028] of Rylander). The device in Rylander is described as a light guiding microneedle that is used for therapy in human tissue (see, for example, paragraph [0161] of Rylander). In addition to delivering light, the microneedles may be used to deliver particulate nanomaterials (e.g., photoabsorbers) into tissue (see, for example, paragraphs [0283], [0295], and [0297] of Rylander). Paragraph [0309] of Rylander describes, for example, that photoabsorbers, such as single walled carbon nanohorns, may be dispended to a bladder using a hollow core fiber microneedle and syringe. Such nanomaterials, however, are not attached to the end portion of the member, as recited in independent claim 1.

Rylander furthermore teaches that such microneedles are difficult to insert into the skin, and thus, a support member for increasing the critical buckling force of the needle(s) to fortify the needles for insertion into the skin is taught, for example, in paragraph [0228]. Rylander describes the microneedle may be embedded inside an elastic medium, such as a polymer (see, for example, paragraph [0216]). Other examples include a guidance ferrule template and an elastomeric support material for increasing the buckling force of the needle(s) (see, for example, paragraphs [0035] and [0155]). In addition, FIG. 1 of Rylander schematically shows that the microneedle is directly inserted into skin, and FIG. 4 of Rylander provides a series of photographic images of a microneedle inserted into kin.

Under such conditions, it is not seen how or why one of ordinary skill in the art would have had any motivation or rational reason to attach a particle onto the microneedle described in Rylander, or would have been able to do so with a reasonable expectation of success. Given such forces (which are described in detail in paragraphs [0217]-[0224] of Rylander), any such particle attached to the microneedle in Rylander would have been removed from (e.g., "scraped off") the

microneedle as it was inserted into the skin. Thus, there would have been no rational or logical reason for adding a particle to the microneedle of Rylander. Instead, the reasonable expectation would have been that adding any such particles to the microneedle of Rylander would have been a futile exercise, since there would have been no way to prevent those particles from being removed from the microneedle, and therefore lost, as the microneedle is inserted into human skin.

In addition, with respect to Szunerits or Hosokawa, it is not seen where either of these would have overcome the deficiencies of Rylander in order to reach the claims. For instance, nowhere do either of Szunerits or Hosokawa teach or suggest attaching a particle to a microneedle in such a way as to keep it from becoming "scraped off' while the microneedle is inserted into the skin, as taught in Rylander. Both Szunerits and Hosokawa appear to be directed to detection techniques using metal particles, but neither of these references would have been useful in preventing particles attached to the microneedles from becoming lost as the microneedles were inserted into the skin as taught in Rylander. Thus, one of ordinary skill in the art would have been discouraged from making the proposed combination, as techniques for detecting particles on a microneedle are useless if the particles are no longer there.
Accordingly, it is not seen how or why one of ordinary skill in the art would have been

motivated to combine Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa to arrive at a particle attached to the end portion of the member, as is recited in independent claim 1. Thus, for at least the reasons outlined above, the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa does not render independent claim 1 obvious, and claim 1 is patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa. The remaining claims that stand rejected on this ground depend from claim 1 and are therefore also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa for at least the reasons outlined above. In addition, it is not conceded that Rylander, Szunerits, or Hosokawa, alone or in combination, teach or render obvious any of the features recited in claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 43, 47, or 135-141, as asserted by the Patent Office. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.

In view of the foregoing, this application should now be in condition for allowance. A notice to this effect is respectfully requested.
